hints.content: To determine the point on the unit circle that corresponds to angle $\theta$, we start from the point $(1,0)$ and move counterclockwise along the circle until the angle that is formed between our position, the origin, and the positive $x$-axis is equal to $\theta$.

Let's take point $A$. The angle it forms with the positive $x$-axis is between $0$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, and it is closer to $0$ than $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. So an appropriate value is $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$.

Point A is located at near two o'clock on the circle. Point B is located near twelve thirty o'clock on the circle. Point C is located near seven o'clock on the circle. A line segment extends from (zero, zero) to point A. An angle from the arc starting at (one, zero) and opening counter clockwise to point A has an angle measurement of pi over five radians.

hints.content:
Point $B$ also forms with the positive $x$-axis an angle that is between $0$ and $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. This time, the point is closer to $\dfrac{\pi}{2}$. So an appropriate value is $\dfrac{3\pi}{7}$.

A line segment extends from (zero, zero) to point B. An angle from the arc starting at (one, zero) and opening counter clockwise to point B has an angle measurement of three pi over seven radians.

hints.content:
Point $C$ forms with the positive $x$-axis an angle that is between $\pi$ and $\dfrac{3\pi}{2}$, so an appropriate value is $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$.

A line segment extends from (zero, zero) to point C. An angle from the arc starting at (one, zero) and opening counter clockwise to point C has an angle measurement of four pi over three radians.

hints.content:
In conclusion, this is the correct answer:

Point | Angle
:-: | :-:
$A$ | $\dfrac{\pi}{5}$
$B$ | $\dfrac{3\pi}{7}$
$C$ | $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$
